Rice, beans, potatoes, bananas, carrots, oats and lentils are cheap foods, and they're vegan. What's expensive is some store products that imitate meat or cheese. But nobody needs them to be vegan. And there's a price that doesn't show up in the shop: to become food, the animal pays with their own life.

text.bold: 1. The basis of a vegan diet is cheap.

paragraph.text: The foods that make up a healthy vegan diet are among the cheapest, and many are already staples of traditional cuisines around the world.

Springmann and colleagues analyzed diets in 150 countries and concluded that vegetarian and vegan variants were generally the most affordable of the healthy and sustainable diets, with cost reductions of up to about 22% to 34% in upper-middle and high-income countries.
No one needs vegan cheese to be vegan, just as no one needs imported cheese to eat cheese.
In many places, protein from beans and lentils costs a fraction of protein from meat.
In low-income countries, healthy diets in general cost more than current diets, which is a problem of poverty, not of veganism.

text.bold: 6. Meat seems cheap because it doesn't pay what it costs.

paragraph.text: It receives subsidies and tax exemptions, and its price doesn't include pollution, emissions, antibiotic resistance and disease risk, which society pays in other ways. According to a 2021 report by FAO, UNDP and UNEP, support to agricultural producers worldwide amounts to about 540 billion dollars a year, and most of it distorts prices or causes harm. And the gravest cost, the suffering and death of animals, isn't counted at all (see J3).

text.bold: 7. The price to the buyer isn't the cost to the one who is eaten.

paragraph.text: Even if meat were cheaper than beans, the comparison would measure only what comes out of the eater's pocket. For the animals, the account is different. According to FAO data compiled by Our World in Data, about 88 billion land animals were slaughtered for meat worldwide in 2024, not counting fish or the animals killed in egg and milk production. These animals pay with their lives, and many, before that, with weeks, months or years of confinement and suffering. A saving on the plate, where there is one, is paid in money; the difference for the animal is paid with a life.

paragraph.text: If a vegan diet can be cheaper, the cost argument doesn't justify eating animals. And even where it cost a little more, the comparison would still be incomplete: on one side, some extra money for the buyer; on the other, the suffering and life of the one who is eaten. The moral question remains: for those who can choose what they eat, what justifies choosing the option that requires someone's death?

It's true that many processed vegan products are expensive, and that price is a real barrier for those who depend on them. It's also true that in some places access to fresh, varied food is limited (J2).

But the basis of vegan eating is made up of some of the cheapest foods there are. For most people, veganism can cost less, not more. And when it does cost more, the difference is paid in money; for the animal, the price of the other choice is their life.
